# An exact six-piece reduction for the joint section-profile functional

This is a finite reduction for two ordinary planar section profiles. It
does not reduce them to triangle tents and does not assert the desired
whole-cap inequality for the resulting six-piece profiles.

## 1. The functional and its actual convex-body realization

Let f,g be nonnegative concave upper-semicontinuous functions on compact
intervals I=[a,b], J=[c,d] of positive lengths. Their closed hypograph
bodies are

    E_f={(s,y):s in I, |y|<=f(s)/2},
    E_g={(s,y):s in J, |y|<=g(s)/2}.

Assume integral f=integral g=1 and integral s f(s) ds=integral s g(s) ds=0.
Thus the two convex bodies have area1 and centroid0. Values at support
endpoints are the actual closed-body section values. Put M=(E_f+E_g)/2.
For a fixed real alpha define

    J_alpha(f,g)=|M intersect {s>=0}|
                    +integral_alpha^infinity f(s) ds
                    +integral_(-alpha)^infinity g(s) ds.             (1)

Profiles are zero outside their support intervals only when computing
these integrals. At an endpoint a nonempty zero-length section remains
available in the Minkowski sum. This is exactly the sharp planar
supremal-section functional of the preceding triangle-profile source.

## 2. Fixed knots: the objective is affine on finite slope-order cells

Fix knots a=x_0<...<x_N=b and c=y_0<...<y_L=d. Allow the values of
f and g at these knots to vary, with linear interpolation between knots.
Impose nonnegativity, concavity, the two unit-mass constraints and the
two zero-first-moment constraints. The resulting feasible set P is a
polytope. It is compact: mass is a positive linear combination of the
nonnegative knot heights (the trapezoidal weights are positive), so
each height is bounded. It is nonempty whenever an initial pair is given.

Partition P by all comparisons

    (f(x_i)-f(x_(i-1)))/(x_i-x_(i-1))
          <=,=,>=
    (g(y_j)-g(y_(j-1)))/(y_j-y_(j-1)).                 (2)

These are finitely many linear hyperplanes in the height coordinates.
Each closed cell is therefore a compact polytope. On a cell, the
decreasing order in which the upper edges of E_f and E_g merge in
their Minkowski sum is fixed. For a tie choose either order: the two
edges are parallel, and the inserted intermediate point is collinear.
Every upper vertex of M in this fixed edge sequence has an abscissa
equal to (x_i+y_j)/2, independent of the heights, and an ordinate affine
in the heights. The initial upper endpoint is affine as well, even
when the endpoint heights are allowed to vary.

The area of M above s=0 is affine on this cell. Integrate each linear
roof segment between its fixed abscissae. If zero cuts a segment, its
interpolation fraction depends only on those fixed abscissae. Upper
and lower symmetry gives the full section length; no new moving cut
abscissa appears. Each endpoint integral in(1) is also linear in its
profile heights, because its integration threshold and axial knots are
fixed. Hence J_alpha is AFFINE jointly in both height vectors on every
closed slope-order cell, including tied slopes and a cut through a
vertex. This is stronger than merely saying it is convex in one profile.

It follows that a minimum of J_alpha on P can be selected at a vertex
of one of these cells. Indeed finitely many compact cells cover P;
on any cell an affine functional attains a minimum at a vertex. For
completeness, the latter statement follows by taking a minimizing point
in a face of smallest dimension: if that face had positive dimension,
a short segment in its affine hull would keep the value minimal, and
extending it to the boundary would give a smaller-dimensional minimizing
face, a contradiction.

## 3. Exact rank count: at most six affine pieces in each profile

At such a selected vertex, merge consecutive collinear profile segments.
Let m and r be the resulting numbers of distinct affine pieces of f and g.
Their slopes are strictly decreasing between the retained pieces. The
space of height perturbations preserving every active within-profile
collinearity relation has dimension m+r+2: the retained m+1 and r+1
vertex heights are free, with original intermediate heights recovered
by linear interpolation. This statement concerns fixed abscissae only.

Every interior knot height is strictly positive. A nonnegative concave
profile of positive integral is positive at every interior point, by
interpolating a point of positive height with both endpoints. Thus the
only possible active nonnegativity constraints occur at the four
support endpoints. Let z be the number of zero endpoint heights,
so0<=z<=4. They impose at most z independent linear equations.
The mass and first-moment constraints impose at most four more.

Finally an active cross-slope equality in(2) identifies one distinct
slope of f with one distinct slope of g. Because each reduced profile's
slopes are strictly decreasing, these identifications form an
order-preserving partial matching. Repetitions among original collinear
pieces give duplicate equations. Therefore their rank is at most
k<=min(m,r).

If m+r+2-z-4-k were positive, there would be a nonzero height direction
preserving all active equations just listed. All remaining finitely
many inequalities are strict; sufficiently small perturbations in BOTH
directions would remain in the same cell of P. This contradicts vertexhood.
Consequently

    m+r-2-z<=k<=min(m,r),
    max(m,r)<=2+z<=6.                                  (3)

This proves: with fixed support knots, masses and means, there is a pair
of profiles, each with at most six affine pieces, whose joint functional
does not exceed that of the original pair. No simplex/tent extreme-point
principle is invoked. In particular, slope matches between the two profiles
are explicitly retained rather than discarded as nongeneric events.

One may instead fix all four endpoint heights to their original values.
The perturbation dimension is then m+r-2; the same four moment equations
and at most min(m,r) slope matches give max(m,r)<=6 again. This variant
preserves the endpoint heights exactly on the finite knot set. When they
are free, (3) gives the additional finite-polytope refinement max(m,r)<=2+z.

## 4. Arbitrary concave profiles: a rigorous limiting reduction

For each initial f,g choose increasingly fine knot partitions of their
support intervals and linearly interpolate their actual values. These
concave piecewise-affine functions converge uniformly on the closed
intervals. To justify endpoint continuity, upper-semicontinuity gives
the upper bound at an endpoint, while concavity against any fixed interior
point gives the matching lower limit. Continuity on the interior is the
ordinary finite concave-function property. Thus the interpolated masses
tend to1 and their first moments tend to0.

Normalize each interpolant by dividing its height by its mass, and
translate its axial coordinate by minus its own mean. These operations
restore EXACT area1 and centroid0. The two support intervals have the
same widths as the original intervals and translate by amounts tending
to zero. Their convex bodies converge in Hausdorff distance to E_f,E_g.
For the fixed alpha, the corresponding objectives converge to(1).

Apply the finite-knot theorem to each normalized pair. Write F_n,G_n
for its replacing symmetric convex bodies. Each has area1, centroid0,
the same support interval as its respective normalized input, and an
upper profile with at most six nonvertical affine pieces. Their heights
are uniformly bounded: a concave nonnegative function on an interval
of width w has integral at least w times its maximum height divided
by2, by the two triangles joining a maximizing point to the support
endpoints. With unit integral its maximum is at most2/w.

Represent each upper profile by its at most seven ordered graph vertices,
padding by repeated vertices if necessary. All these coordinates lie in
a common compact rectangle. Passing to a subsequence, every vertex of
both profiles converges. Taking convex hulls of the limiting upper
vertices and their lower reflections gives limits F_*,G_* in Hausdorff
distance. They retain the two original support intervals, area1 and
centroid0. The area and first moments converge: indicators of bounded
convex bodies converge away from the limit boundary, which has planar
measure zero, so bounded convergence applies. In particular the limit
bodies remain full-dimensional.

Their upper boundaries have at most six nonvertical affine pieces.
Adjacent vertices can coalesce in abscissa and produce a vertical support
face; discarding the lower point on such a face cannot increase the
number of nonvertical edges. We do NOT assume that the original endpoint
height values pass to the limit. A short segment can collapse into a
larger supporting face. The closed limiting body supplies its actual
endpoint values.

Minkowski addition and averaging preserve Hausdorff convergence directly:
approximate each summand point within its Hausdorff error, and add the
errors. Intersections with the fixed halfplane have convergent area,
again by bounded convergence outside convex boundaries and the cutting
line. The same applies to the two fixed endpoint halfplanes at alpha
and-alpha. Therefore

    J_alpha(F_*,G_*)
        =lim J_alpha(F_n,G_n)
        <=lim J_alpha(normalized input profiles)
        =J_alpha(f,g).                                  (4)

Here J_alpha of a symmetric body means the functional of its actual
vertical section profile. This proves an exact replacement for each
given pair and each fixed tilt, without assuming a global minimizer over
unbounded support widths exists and without interchanging an infimum
with a limit.

## 5. Precise scope

For the all-profile inequality J_alpha>=4/3, a counterexample among
arbitrary area-one centered concave planar profiles exists if and only
if one exists among pairs having at most six affine pieces each. The
forward implication is the proved replacement; the reverse is immediate.
This is a finite-complexity reduction, not a proof of that inequality.
The exact tent result only handles at most two pieces per profile and
does not automatically extend to the six-piece class. In fact the
unrestricted target is FALSE: the exact constant-profile rectangle
certificate in constant-profile-rectangle-obstruction-to-universal-three-
grunbaum-credit-two-sided.md gives J=21/16<4/3. Both profiles there
already have only one affine piece. Thus this target is closed by a
counterexample; the finite reduction remains available for other,
correctly scoped inequalities.

The construction retains the whole midpoint-section contribution and
both endpoint tails at the SAME fixed alpha. It preserves ordinary
area and the actual continuous centroids. It concerns the sharp symmetric
profile realization of one chosen continuous direction; it does not
claim a body replacement that preserves every other angular depth or a
single profile deformation working simultaneously for all directions.
